utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have the appearances for the day, please, starting with Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Your Honours, and firstly an apology for keeping everybody waiting for a few moments this morning. I'd received wrong information that we were starting at quarter past, but I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Barney Thomas, April Carter, and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Gregor Guy-Smith, Chad Mair, and Tina Drolec appearing on behalf of Mr. Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, we would call our next witness, if we could, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: For the Court's information, the next witness is General Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Surely. If I could have the court usher grab this yellow binder for a moment so that the Prosecution can take a quick look. I'll wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, you may be seated, sir. Good morning to you, sir. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If the court usher would be so kind as to grab the yellow binder the Prosecution has had an opportunity to review.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: Morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you'd tell us your name and spell your last name for the record, we'd appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning. My name is Radojica Kadijevic. Lieutenant-General, retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Since you are retired, would you prefer that I call you Mr. Kadijevic or General? What is your preference, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: It makes no difference to me. Whatever suits you best.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. Probably during the course of our conversation today I'll probably end up calling you both, so ... How long have you been retired?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: For 11 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And prior to your retirement, for whom did you work, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: Before my retirement, I was assistant federal minister for defence for military economic activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I was on the wrong channel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, it's fine. I have an opportunity to read it, it just took me a moment. And for how long a period of time were you the assistant federal minister for defence for the military economic activities?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: I was appointed assistant federal minister in June 1995, and I stayed in that position until April 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Prior to your appointment as assistant federal minster for defence for military economic activities, what post did you hold, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: Prior to that I was chief of the administration for investigation, development, manufacture of weaponry and military equipment within the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And for how long a period of time did you hold that post?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: I held the post of chief for research, development, and manufacture from November 1993 until the following position that I took.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And before you were the chief for research and development for manufacture in the Ministry of Defence what post did you hold, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: Prior to that I was the chief of the navy and technical administration within the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia, and prior to that, Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And could you tell us what time-period you were involved in that post?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: I held the post of the chief of the navy and technical administration for five years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if we were to go back in time, would that be then starting in 1987?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Upon completing the national school of -- for defence, I was appointed chief of the navy and technical administration, which was attached to the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And without going through each and every other post that you held while you were working before your retirement, when did you first join the military?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: I first joined the army in 1992 upon graduating from the navy and technical academy in Pula. Prior to that I was a cadet and I attended the navy and technical academy for three years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether or not you misspoke or you misheard but it indicates that you first joined the army in 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, it was a slip of the tongue. It was in 1962.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If it was the slip of the tongue, then did you graduate in the navy and technical academy just prior to 1962? Because you were interpreted as saying you first joined the army in 1992 upon graduating in the technical academy -- in the navy and technical academy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's possible that it was a mistake. I applied and was admitted into the navy and technical academy in 1959. The academy lasted three years and I graduated in September of 1962. According to our regulation, one is promoted into the rank of 2nd lieutenant on the day one joins the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When were you born, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 17th of April, 1940.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: I was born in a place called Glavina Donja, municipality of Iv Imotski, Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you ever serve in any other military organisations apart from the JNA, the VJ, and the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: No, sir. I never served in any other organisation other than the JNA, the Army of Yugoslavia, and my last position was with the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were you ever asked to or ordered to serve in any other military organisations apart from the JNA, the VJ, and the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: No, nobody asked me to do that nor have I ever had problems with that type of request. I was transferred from the General Staff to the Ministry of Defence and I had regular promotions there until I reached the position of assistant minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to spend a moment or two dealing with your duties from June 1995 to 1999 when you were the assistant minister of defence. Could you please tell us what your responsibilities were while you were in that position.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: The main task in that position was to co-ordinate within the sector for military economic activities in order to fulfill the duties and obligations of the Army of Yugoslavia when it comes to funding, equipment, and weaponry. In order to complete my task, I was superior to the institute for research and development of the Army of Yugoslavia, and it dealt with research and development as well as the development of the special military industry -- special-purpose military industry, which was to produce the equipment and weaponry needed for the military. In addition to that, within the sector there was an administration for procurement of military equipment and weaponry and that administration procured within the country and also abroad whatever was needed for the Ministry of Defence and the Army of Yugoslavia. In order to ensure all of that, there was a department for quality control of weaponry and military equipment as well as department for standardisation and nomenclature in which ensured that everything was of a good quality and given as such to the end users, and they also prepared the system that was meant to service and repair that equipment. In addition to this, there was also the field of international military and scientific corporation and a lot of people within the ministry and the army took part in this corporation. This corporation was co-ordinated and headed by us, by my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to your duties when you were in the position of assistant minister of defence, after Dayton, and we'll touch upon this later in your testimony, were you also appointed to a commission dealing with demilitarisation in the region and specifically with the demilitarisation of FRY?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: By way of a decision of the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia I was appointed chairman of the commission which was tasked with implementing in full the Florence Agreement. Pursuant to the decision of the prime minister of the federal government, the tasks of both me and members of the commission were fully defined. We had no opportunity to do anything else other than strictly implement the agreement on disarmament that had been signed. In that position, or rather in that capacity, I especially emphasised to other members of the commission that I would never accept any sort of interference of politics into the implementation of the agreement. The federal government tasked us to report back to them each month about the activities that we undertook and how they proceeded.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel be asked to switch off microphone when not in use. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you for that response. We'll have further discussion about this particular endeavour later on in your testimony, but I thank you for that response at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, you heard the request from the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to, at this point in time, based upon the answer that you've given us, take a look at a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could please have D240 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That will be the first document, the very first tab in your binder, sir. And this is a document called "Rules On The Responsibilities Of The Organisational Units In The Defence Ministry." We discussed this document and I understand that you are familiar with it. Could you please take a look at Article" 15 of this document, which defines the duties, sector for military economic activity, which I believe is on page -- on page 9 of the English, I believe page 7 of the B/C/S. I believe.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just for the record, B/C/S page number 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I do apologise. Page number 8. Article 15.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Page 10 for you, yes. There is an electronic system, a hard copy system, a B/C/S system, an English system; everything is differently paginated but I'm sure we'll all get to the same page eventually. Could you take a look at the Article 15, please, sir. If you could, could you confirm for us if it is accurate that those were the duties and responsibilities of the sector for military activity, economic activity of the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, those were, in general, the tasks of the sector for military economic activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the issue of the procurement administration, could you take a look at Article 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that will be on page 10 of the English. And I believe it's going to be in B/C/S and it's going to be page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you have the section entitled "Procurement Administration"? Right above --

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have found it, and I have looked at it. These are general responsibilities of the procurement administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to spend a moment here. You indicated that between 1993 and 1995 your duties were as the chief of the research and development administration, and if I am not mistaken, that also included the issue of procurement. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think you are quite right because the administration for research, development, and manufacture did not also deal with procurement. The administration for research, development, and manufacture mostly brought together all fields of scientific work for the needs of the army of Yugoslavia and the federal ministry and their component parts. In addition to that, this administration developed facilities for special-purpose industry. They also developed new technologies, approved various investments and investment plans, and they also drafted regulations which dealt with the field that they were responsible for. In addition to that, the administration also co-operated with other military scientific institutions within the the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the procurement administration, what, if any, involvement did you have with the procurement administration during your tenure as the chief of research and development?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: I had none because these are two parallel administrations at the same level. They co-operated closely between each other, especially when it comes to procurement of new equipment. In those cases, people from the research and development administration would get involved in procurement of this new equipment in order to develop the necessary regulations and paperwork, especially when it it comes to prices, standards, and so on, whereas the procurement administration would take care of the commercial part of those deals. So when it comes to such activities, all sectors would co-operate, all sectors within the military economic activity sectors, just as the quality control administration had its staff both within the Ministry of Defence and within the military industry. They were tasked with ensuring the appropriate standard of equipment in all stages of manufacture so that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: In reviewing Article 17, are you familiar with those -- the tasks that are set forth with regard to what the procurement administration was supposed to be engaged in?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm fully familiar with these tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And as I understand this, looking at the plain language here, it says the procurement administration shall carry out the tasks that pertain to supplying of the VJ with combat and -- I seem to be having some screen problems, that's why you hear my sigh. My screen keeps on going on and off. With combat and non-combat equipment. As such, 1, and I shall not read them all, it says it "shall supply the Yugoslav Army with the weapons and military equipment and other supplies, delivering them to the army depots, procuring them from domestic sources, and shall contract the repair of equipment and materiel." To your understanding was that one of the main functions of the procurement administration?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the basic function of the procurement administration, although it had other tasks as well as listed in here, and that's what they did, however this was the main task and that's hence its name, the procurement administration. There was a time when the title was expanded to the procurement administration, or rather, the procurement of armament and military equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like you to take just a brief look at number 6, where it states: "It shall sell assets within its purview." My question to you here, sir, is could you explain to us what assets, if you know, were within its purview that it had the authority and responsibility to sell?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: The procurement administration, as I said, dealt with the sale of armament and military equipment of different types. Primarily they sold the surpluses of armament and military equipment, obsolete types of armament and military equipment, and later on, when we were engaged in the destruction of military technique pursuant to the disarmament agreement, that technique was all cut to pieces and we sold raw materials, iron and everything else. Whatever the Ministry of Defence and the Army of Yugoslavia advertised as surplus, we in the administration received documents and accompanying materials requesting us to embark on the sale of such supplies because the administration for procurement had staff that knew how to deal with such tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to what you've just said, you indicated that it dealt with the sale of armament and military equipment of different types. My question: Who was the owner of that equipment and who had the right to alienate that equipment?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: The owner of all the equipment and armament in the Army of Yugoslavia and the Ministry of Defence was the federal government pursuant to the Law on Defence; the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the ownership interest and the right to alienate property, what, if any, ownership or rights did the Yugoslav Army have to sell, alienate, hypothecate, give, or transfer property?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: The Army of Yugoslavia in that sense did not have any right to dispose, or rather, alienate the property in any way. The Army of Yugoslavia, when it estimated that a combat system or a piece of equipment was obsolete and unnecessary, had the right to advertise it as unnecessary and to propose that it be written off. When the decision was taken that a piece of equipment was no longer necessary, such pieces of equipment were forwarded to further procedure to the Ministry of Defence which then made the decision to decommission or sell such a piece of equipment, and the proceeds of such a sale were transferred into the federal budget.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could now take a look at Article 23, which deals with finance and budget administration. It will be on page 14 in the English, and I'm not going to hazard a guess as to what page it will be in B/C/S at this moment in the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 16. 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, during the time that you were the assistant minister of defence pertaining to economic activities, is Article 23 an article that you concerned yourself with?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: This article did not relate to me. There was a special administration and the chief of that administration, who was directly subordinated to the federal minister of defence. Obviously by virtue of my position, I co-operated with the chief of that administration because we had to co-ordinate activities in the implementation of certain programmes. There was always a problem of the lack of resources, lack of money, and our dynamics of investment in military capacities and the adoption of new technologies is something that I had to co-ordinate with the chief of that administration in order for the financial resources to be able to follow the process of production and adoption and procurement of new technologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the requirements that are set forth in this particular article, are you familiar with these requirements?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, did you have the whole article in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: I was familiar with all that because I co-operated with the chief of the administration, I was in daily contact with him, we shared the experiences, we shared each other's problems, so I was basically familiar with the work and the scope of his work and activities, but I did not have anything to do, I did not have any authorities with this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's understood. And without going through each and every article, would it be fair to say that you had familiarity and are aware of the requirements that are set forth in this particular document?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. One might say so. As I've already pointed out, I encountered the same problems that the chief of the administration for finances and budget had.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I ask for this document's admission. I'm sorry, it's in, Your Honour. It's in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: At the outset of your testimony you indicated that you were in the JNA and you were also in the VJ and the Ministry of Defence. I'd like to discuss with you for a moment, first of all, when did you cease being in the VJ and become a member of -- I'm sorry, cease being a member of the JNA and become a participant in the VJ? What year was that?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: That happened in 1992, I suppose, after the transformation. The process of transformation started in 1987 while the JNA was still in place. We had a lot of transformation cycles. For example, the ones after 1995 and then after 1996, everything that had been done up to then was done in a haste. In practice it was proven that such a structure of the Main Staff and the Ministry of Defence was not adequate because they were not conducive to -- to the efficient of work of neither of the organs. I apologise for having to add this as well: I believe that that transformation was not such a clear-cut so as to enable one to know that as of today, for example, one is a member of the Army of Yugoslavia. Regulations that were in effect in the JNA continued to be used because there were simply no new regulations in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, I think that answer goes far beyond your question. If you could try and curtail the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the system of defence, and by that I mean the broad system of defence that existed before the transformation, could you describe for us what that system was? And by that I mean at the high level of the relationship between the Ministry of Defence and the army, before the transformation. Was it a unified system; was it a divided system; how would you characterise that system? And keeping in mind His Honour's admonition. It's early in the day, I'll try to make my questions short, and if you would try to make your answers short, I'm sure, among other things, we will please not only ourselves but also the Court.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: During the JNA period, the organisation of the Federal Secretariat for the National Defence represented a single system that also encompassed the General Staff and the entire JNA in depth. After the transformation, there was a separation into two different organisational units. First there was a General Staff which was subordinated to the Supreme Council of Defence and the Federal Ministry of Defence which was subordinated to the federal government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to turn our attention now for a moment in a general sense to another subject you mentioned which is that of special-purpose industries. And if you could describe for us, before the transformation, a couple of matters with regard to. Special-purpose industries. First of all, could you tell us if you know approximately how many special-purpose industries there were?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: In the SFRY there was a military industry and it was very developed and it was part of the so-called Zinvoj association which dealt with the military industry and production, and I believe that there were 120 companies in total which were members of that association, and they are also outsourcing companies that were under the same umbrella. They were all tied to the military economic sector in the federal Secretariat of Defence. During the existence of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia this was reduced to some 12 to 14 companies that belonged to the special-purpose industry which were not well-defined and by inertia they were leaned on the military economic sector of the Federal Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a moment. With regard to the military industry, when you use the term "military industry" are you referring to the military -- a military industrial complex that produces military products for sale?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: There's a serious problem even today with regard to the terminology separating military industry, military industrial complex, special-purpose industry, but this is all the result of the inertia which existed before. The system changed and the names persisted although they don't reflect the current situation. Even in the new Law on Defence, they are not defined as either special-purpose industry or military industry. They are defined by the products they produce which are of some special interest. There may be other civilian companies that they have nothing to do with the Ministry of Defence or the military and they still may be engaged in the production of the same products.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreter is having great difficulty keeping pace with you. Can you slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think I understand your frustration over the topic because it's something that is of concern to you, and we all have a tendency, when dealing with things that are of concern to us, to speed up in our answer, so if you keep that in mind. With regard to this issue, and I'm going to use the term "special-purpose industry" if that's acceptable. With regard to the issue of the special-purpose industry in the the SFRY, was the special-purpose industry an integrated industry, was it a competing industry? How would you characterise the industry before the break-up, or as you've put it, transformation?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: In the SFRY that industry was very well organised, exceptionally organised, and was integrated into an association, and as a result of that there was direct co-operation and there was no unloyal competition. That association was a very complex organisation that also actively sought out jobs and work for the association members. They even had their own administration. And they were transformed into a very complex body. I personally had a lot of problem with that body once that body was abolished.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During the period of time of the SFRY, was the -- were the facilities that produced under the special-purpose industry located in one republic, in one area or region of the former Yugoslavia, or were they located throughout former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: During that period, the state policy dictated the deployment of the military industry companies across the territory of the former state. However, for strategic reasons, most of the military industry was developed and located in Bosnia and Herzegovina and then in Serbia. After that, Croatia and Slovenia. Montenegro and Macedonia lacked behind. They had only very few available capacities and facilities which enabled them to co-operate with the rest of the special-purpose industry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a factory or special-purpose industry by the name of Pretis?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course I'm familiar with that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Where was it located?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: Pretis was near Sarajevo, in a place called Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: After the transformation, in what state or region was Pretis located?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: Pretis remained in the territory that later on became Republika Srpska. We are talking about huge facilities that could not physically be moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to take, if we could, for example, the production of a tank. Could you tell us, if you know, approximately how many production facilities in special-purpose industries within the former Yugoslavia would be involved in the production of a single tank?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: The production of a tank, which was a very complex piece of equipment, required the engagement of a number of companies and outsources. When the state leadership of the SFRY made a decision or was in the process of decision-making for the production of a tank, the basic problem was to establish who would be the final link in the production chain. The political structure played a role in that and there was a struggle for their own republic to take the lead. When it was decided that the production would take place in Croatia, to be more specific in Slavonski Brod in the Djuro Djakovic company, in order to make everybody happy, the outsourcing jobs were assigned to companies from all the other republics in that Croatia had a lot less facilities engaged as outsources in order to strike a balance in the involvement of all the republics of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. If I might, could you by any fashion tell us the approximate number of different production facilities that were involved in this? Five, ten, a hundred, two?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: If my memory serves me well, because I also participated in all that, I believe that a total of 120 companies from all over Yugoslavia participated in that production process.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before the transformation, could you tell us, if you know, approximately how much money was derived from military production in the former Yugoslavia? And I'm talking about on an annual basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Derived by who?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Derived from military production for the benefit of the state. Actually, derived from military production, the gross receipts from production. If he knows.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that most of the exports of armament and equipment and the monitoring of the incoming flows from the sale of equipment and military construction, the latter also being a big source of income, most that was made from all that was about $2 billion in one year.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: After the transformation and specifically in the calendar years of 1993 through 1995, could you tell us, if you know, what the incoming flows from military construction and sales of equipment in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia were?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand your question properly. Are you talking only about exports or are you talking about the domestic sales in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I put my question badly. Let's deal with exports first and then with domestic sales, unless it's easier to put them together for your purposes.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: During that period there was no exports. What was done was probably done illegally, unbeknownst to the Ministry of Defence, I suppose. During that period there was practically no earnings from exports, and when it comes to the deliveries to the Army of Yugoslavia, those deliveries were at a very low level, not because the companies were not able to produce armament and military equipment but because the federal budget did not have enough allocation for the Ministry of Defence and for the military. There was simply not enough money in the budget. For a few years in a row, the participation, or rather the allocation for the armament and military equipment was approximately 10 per cent of the budget. That was allocated for the army and the Ministry of Defence. However, when it came to the reality of the facts, that was even lower, much below the 10 per cent, because the budget allocations did not follow the dynamics of the army requirements and the military was therefore forced to prioritise differently and put emphasis on food, clothing, and medical treatment. That's what the needs that they had to meet first, and then if there were any surpluses, they could be allocated towards the procurement of armament and military equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Obviously, as you've discussed, the number of special-purpose industries that existed in the former Yugoslavia were diminished once the creation of FRY occurred. Can you tell us, if you know, the number of workers that were dependent in the former -- sorry, in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on the special-purpose industry? By that, those that were -- how many were employed in that industry?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: Companies from the list of the federal government that were part of the special-purpose industry initially employed 30.000 workers and later on 28.000 workers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to those 30.000 workers that were employed by the special-purpose industry, if you know once again, was the Ministry of Defence in a position to engage in sufficient contracts to keep those individuals gainfully employed?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: The Federal Ministry of Defence had only had funds coming in from the budget in order to sign contracts with the companies from the special-purpose industry. There were years when we had no contracts whatsoever with some of the companies from that industry. Practically, the federal ministry did not engage in any contracts with them sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did this constitute an economic problem for the special-purpose industries in your country, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: It was wasn't just an economic problem, it was a social one as well because many families depended on what those people earned in those companies, so it was a political problem as well. And in addition to that, it was a technological problem because they started falling out of pace, there were no further investments, they could not modernise the company, the manufacturing plants and so on, so that industry was practically devastated and deteriorated greatly in comparison to what it used to be prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You indicated earlier, with regard to the issue of exports, at page 21, line 1, you said during that period, and it was referring to the period of 1993 through 1995, there were no exports, what was done was probably done illegally, unbeknownst to the Ministry of Defence. And I'd like to spend a moment or two with you on that particular aspect of your answer. With regard to the issue of exports, could you tell us what the technically proper way for a special-purpose industry to engage in exporting military goods would be? What is the procedure?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: The sales of armament and military equipment, both in the country and abroad, was regulated by law. The procedures were clear and fully regulated. However, during the economic sanctions, these procedures were not always complied with. Directors of companies, in order to ensure survival for their companies, found other exporters rather than the approved federal institution because they wanted to make sure that there would be export and that their company would survive. The exports that went via SDPER, the federally approved organ for exports, were all legal. They went with appropriate approvals and so on. However --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. You've used a -- you've used some letters and we just need to understand what those letters are. You've used the letters SDPER. Could you tell us what that stands for, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: It stands for federal directorate for sales of goods -- of special-purpose goods. This was the organ that existed back in the times SFRY but at the time it was called Yugo Import. The federal government issued a decision to establish a particular body that would deal with these matters, and this was a body that existed within the federal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You said that they went with appropriate approvals and so on. With regard to the issue of exports, and specifically when you say appropriate approvals, what kind of approvals are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: In order for the goods to be exported according to the law, the federal defence ministry was responsible for authorising it, for issuing permits for those transactions. These permits, among other things, were needed for the customs to let such goods through so that these goods could cross the border. In addition to that, the permits were needed for the Ministry of the Interior to allow transport of such goods via the state territory. It was all strictly regulated. All movements of such goods were, and these goods could not be taken over without being checked prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue of export of material, you've mentioned customs and you've mentioned the minister -- the Ministry of the Interior. What involvement, if any, did the VJ have in exporting goods, under the law?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: Under the law, the Army of Yugoslavia and the General Staff had no competencies when it came to exports of military equipment, military goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue of the Ministry of the Interior, what specifically were the duties and obligations of the Ministry of the Interior with regard to the export of military goods?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior regulated only the transport and movement of dangerous goods within the territory of our own country. No transport could take place within the country from one special-purpose company to the other special company to the army warehouses without there being a prior approval issued by the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to customs, what was customs' involvement with regard to the exportation of military goods?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: The customs played its standard role when it comes to any goods; they checked entry and export of any goods to ensure that they had proper documentation. The permits issued by the Ministry of the Interior was sufficient to let these goods cross the border. If there were no permits, the goods were not allowed to cross. Before such permits were issued -- I forgot to tell you that, before export permits were issued, the opinion of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs was needed. Ministry of Foreign Affairs, in accordance with its responsibilities, had to ensure whether there was any resolution of UN Security Council restricting importation of military goods. If the Ministry of Foreign Affairs thought that there were any problems, they would not issue their approval and then no export permits would be issued at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take the break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could -- if you could turn to tab number 6, which is P597. One of the things we were talking about before the break was the movement of goods. Could you take a look at what should be at tab number 6, which is P597, which is entitled "Dispatch Note Number 115." Do you see that document? Should be behind tab number 6.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you tell us what this document is, please, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: By way of this document, the factory called Krusik Valjevo sends goods, in this case it is the Drina Corps, headquartered in Vlasenica, and this is a receipt that accompanies the goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What involvement, if any, does the VJ have with regard to this particular transaction?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: In this particular transaction, the Army of Yugoslavia has no role. Moreover, the Ministry of Defence has no role in this either.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Take a look at the next tab in your binder, tab number 7, which is P598. Could you tell us what this document is, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: This is a similar document, again a dispatch note, the Krusik Valjevo factory, special-purpose factory, sends goods to a certain military post in Vlasenica as well. The Army of Yugoslavia and the Ministry of Defence had nothing to do with this transaction either.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you now turn to tab number 22 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Which is -- I apologise, which is OTP 65 ter 742.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it not yet admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It is not. It's on our 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it going to be coming in as a Defence exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 65 ter OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you some questions about this document. Could you tell us who this document is coming from?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: You mean tab 22?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: This document was used within the Army of Republika Srpska. Chief of the technical service addresses the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff of the VRS in this document. So this is a document that was used between the Main Staff and one of the subordinate institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Can you tell us the date of this document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Say that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you tell us the date of this document, please?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: This document is dated 16 March 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In the text of the document, at least in the English translation, it says: "For a repair of a T-55/a tank/(2 vehicles) and a 90 mm SO/self-propelled gun/M36 B-1 (one vehicle) we are hereby asking you to secure an approval through the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Serbia for a maintenance ... " then the document continues. With regard to the Ministry of Defence that is being referred to here, is that your Ministry of Defence or some other Ministry of Defence, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: I know that this is the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska. In this document they ask for approval that a certain equipment be repaired in the repair shop in Hadzici in Republika Srpska, and if not possible, then they ask that the repairs be conducted in Cacak in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The subordinate organ uses routine channels to address the Main Staff so that the Main Staff can address directly the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska, because the author of this document was not allowed to directly contact the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska. He had to go via the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My question to you here is it says here, it says, we are hereby asking you to secure an approval through the Ministry of Defence of Republic of Serbia. Is that translation incorrect? Is it the Republika Srpska or is it the Republic of Serbia that is being referred to here?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: Republika Srpska only, because the repair facility is in Hadzici and they seek approval because the Ministry of Defence had to approve the repair.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I move its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, just before we admit it, let's just get the record clear. The English translation here reads "through the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Serbia." You are saying "Republika Srpska." Is that what stands on the B/C/S version? Or in other words, is the English translation incorrect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the translation is incorrect because the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Serbia did not exist at this point in time. Only the federal ministry of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia existed at this period in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But my question specifically is what stands on the B/C/S version? What is written on the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the B/C/S version it says Ministry of Defence of RS. "RS" stands for Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: RS; they didn't write the full name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. The document is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D446. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to this particular document, what involvement, if any, did the VJ have with regard to this transaction?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: No. They did not participate nor could they have participated given the methodology of work as it was done at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could now see 65 ter OTP 810, which is tab 23 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Looking at the title of this document indicating Issuance Form, in English it indicates at the very top: "For the below-listed material property items received for temporary use from the Ministry of Defence of Republic of Serbia /handwritten/7296 Vlasenica." In B/C/S could you confirm that that is what is written?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: I can confirm that that is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. With regard to this particular document, what involvement, if any, if you know, did the VJ have with regard to the temporary use from the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Serbia, the below-listed item, number one, which are bullets?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is 7.62 round for an automatic rifle, and you see the number 42.560 pieces. That is Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska, and rounds were provided directly to the military post in Vlasenica, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Here is my question: As I look at the translation in English and as I look at the language that is contained in the document at the top in Latinised script in B/C/S, I see that it indicates there's some standard language and then it says Ministarsivo Odbrane Republike Srbije; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That would be the Republic of Serbia, correct? That's what the document says?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What involvement would the VJ have with regard to this particular transaction?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of Defence did not participate, neither did the Army of Yugoslavia because this was property of the Republic of Serbia which followed from the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would move its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D447. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The next document would be 65 ter - this is once again a Prosecution 65 ter number - 815, which is number 24 in your binder, sir. I see the -- yes, now I see the English as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Taking a look at this document, this document is entitled, in English "Delivery Sheet Receipt Note." And it indicates at line number 4 that the sender of this document is the Republic of Serbia Ministry of the Interior. And it's being sent to the Drina Corps command, which would be found in box number 14, which would be the name and address of the receiver. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the transaction, the transaction involves various bullets and grenades; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What involvement, if any, did the VJ have with regard to this transaction?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: The Army of Yugoslavia did not participate in this transaction because this was not about property or equipment that was in the hands of the Army of Yugoslavia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could now turn to 65 ter OTP 816, which would be tab number 25 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you want to do with --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, thank you so much, Your Honours. I'd move its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, it's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this shall be given Exhibit D448. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually, I was going to object to the admission of the document. This -- and it seems that we are going to a series of documents in which the witness is being asked to read in the four corners of the document itself as opposed to having any direct knowledge of the document of the transaction, he has given the general competencies that were at issue of the various ministries, so I don't think there's been an appropriate nexus between this witness and this document or any documents of its kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would tend to disagree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Bases for your disagreement, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We've had discussion with regard to his competencies and authorities. If you want, I can fill it out further, if the Chamber deems it necessary. Why don't I make life easier for everybody, instead? I'll just fill it out a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I can't hear you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I said why don't I fill it out a bit since there seems to be some consternation or confusion, I'm happy to fill it out a bit more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We understand, but the basis of the objection is that the witness has nothing to do with this document, he doesn't know the document. All he can say is that the VJ had nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That in and of itself is certainly relevant to these proceedings. That in and of itself, based upon the kind of evidence we have received here before, and specifically with regard to such issues of material sheets, of which there have been legion material sheets introduced by the Prosecution without the benefit of any oral testimony whatsoever --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The problem being that you are making this witness deny the involvement of the VJ with documents that the Prosecution has not tendered. You are not dealing with documents that were tendered. I'm not quite sure what then is the purpose here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate that. The purpose is actually twofold. One is that, by virtue of the position that the Prosecution holds, and specifically that is not merely to convict but to see that justice is done, they are to give to you a complete -- that being the fact-finders -- a complete and full picture and understanding of the evidence that exists with regard to their case. These documents which were on their list which they were well aware of and are well aware of and were created during the investigation of and preparation of the prosecution of their case are indicative of something which is relatively important with regard to the indictment as charged. And that is, that material, supplies, and specifically such supplies as ammunition, stemmed from other parties and organs apart from the party that they claim was responsible for such supply, that being the VJ. Evidence that establishes such a position and establishes such reality is not only relevant, but is of assistance to the Trial Chamber when it has to make a determination in dealing with the liability of General Perisic as a Chief of Staff of the VJ, and specifically with regard to specific issues concerning the conceptual basis of aiding and abetting. Therefore, I think that there are not only a myriad bases upon which the document is not only relevant but important, but in the fair administration of justice and in fairness to Mr. Perisic's right to trial, this kind of evidence need be considered by the Chamber, and the Prosecution, I would hope and would think, would not resist such information if it takes its duty seriously, and that is to give a full and complete picture to the Chamber of the situation at hand, which I think is something which has been recognised not only by the decision of law of this Tribunal but had been recognised by the decision of law of courts in jurisdictions throughout the world for eons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether -- I would hate to go into dialogue with you. You know, as I understand the charge of aiding and abetting, it presupposes certain actions taken by the perpetrator, and to prove aiding and abetting, it is not -- it's not necessary to enumerate the actions of the perpetrator because it is understood that the perpetrator did perpetrate the crime. What I do find of crucial importance and relevance to a charge of aiding and abetting are the actions of the aider. Now, you are making -- you are casting aspersions on the Prosecution to say they should have told -- put before the Chamber exculpatory material. Now, that would be exculpatory if it was not aiding and abetting. If it is aiding and abetting, it is known that there will be some actions by the perpetrator, but the concern here is with the aider and abetter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, Your Honour, I understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me also finish. I gave you a chance to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So the fact that the VJ had nothing do with these documents, does not negate the allegation that the VJ may or may not have had something to do with some other documents of a similar nature. So I'm not quite sure how helpful these documents are for purposes of aiding and abetting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand what you've said, and I think that to the extent you've articulated part of the analysis in aiding and abetting, we would probably have no disagreement, but the analysis of aiding and abetting goes further than that, and one of the things this Chamber is going to have to determine is the issue of substantiality. And with regard to the issue of substantiality there's going to be at some point some analysis that the Chamber will have to go through, or I assuming would go through, with regard to all of these materiel lists, all of the requests, all of the orders, and what the results of them are. And at some point in time you are going to, I think, make a determination one way or the other as to whether or not the body of that information substantiates the Prosecution's position that these -- that that information and that body of information was sufficient to meet the definition of aiding and abetting. Now, if you have other information and you have other affirmative information that shows that supplies were being given to the Republika Srpska, to the VRS, and to the Republika Srpska Krajina, the SVK, and they were receiving arms, they were receiving ammunition, they were receiving the means of war and they replied upon those means and those arms and that ammunition in order to either, A, prosecute the war, or, B, engage in the perpetration of crimes, and I am not suggesting they did but for the purposes of the discussion we are having right now, then that information is critical to your determination as fact-finders, because you are going to have to make a determination as to whether or not it's substantial or not. For example, here specifically, since we are specifically dealing with the issue of ammunition and an issue that we've talked about for close to two years, on and off, if you are dealing with the issue of ammunition and you have the ability to learn that ammunition came from other sources in large measure during the relevant period of time, one would think that certainly would impact upon the decision-making process that you go through. It certainly would be part and parcel of the analysis that you engage in, is our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. In that event, I hear what you say. Can I make a suggestion then. If perhaps it is your intention to tender all the information relating to other sources of supply other than the VJ in order to shorten the proceedings, are you not going to be giving us all those all in one batch and then let's see them, rather than go one by one like this?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That would be one fashion. First of all, unfortunately, I'm certainly not going to tender all the information relating to other sources, I just want to make that clear, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then we don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to give you -- I'm going to give you as much as I can in the same fashion as the Prosecution has given you as much as they can. Because ultimately what is going to happen here, factually speaking, is you are going to be asked to infer certain things based upon a body of factual information that you have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure, I understand. I'm with you. I'm with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to your suggestion, if I could have but a moment, because I have no desire to lengthen anything whatsoever in terms of the trial. So if I could have but a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just make a ruling on the objection before you do that. The objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask the grounds in regards to the overruling? Because my objection was never a relevance objection, it was a particular nexus between this witness and the document itself. So it seems the discourse that has been had isn't responsive to my immediate objection that there's no nexus between this individual sitting here before us today and the document itself. And I feel if we are going to be batching them, that I'll have the same running objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might quickly respond. By "quickly" I mean quickly. Under the guide-lines 30, I think that we cannot only find guidance but support for the position that has been taken, which says the Trial Chamber shall begin any analysis on the admissibility of evidence by recalling 89(C) of the Rules, which provides that: "A Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value." In Rule 89(D) of the Rules which provides that: "A Chamber may exclude evidence if its probative value is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial." I think that guideline more than adequately covers the particular situation we are in.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the Prosecution is aware of Rule 89(F) that says relevant information should become before the Chamber, the Chamber has always required that there is a nexus between the witness and the document that's being tendered. This isn't a bar table motion, this isn't another witness in which the document can be spoken to. This witness doesn't have those competencies, and so what we are seeing here today is as opposed to using the appropriate vehicle in order to tender these documents into evidence, the Defence has chosen a witness who has no relation to them and are seeking to elevate their status -- taking a General of his great means and trying to elevate his status by having him comment on them, which I don't think is an appropriate use of the Court's time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are talking about the Court's time. Madam Carter, what I do notice in this situation is that the Defence seeks to get the witness who was involved with procurement to tell the Court whether or not the VJ had anything to do with these documents. Now, if the Defence were to tender these documents by way of a bar table motion, they would not have anybody who would confirm. It would have to be testimony by the counsel to say the VJ had nothing to do with these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And I understand that indeed there is no nexus between the documents and the witness and it looks -- it seems to me as if the purpose is precisely to state that lack of nexus.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, if the the witness was a procurement officer, that would be a much different question. The witness was specifically asked on page 10, starting at line 7: "With regard to the procurement administration, what if any involvement did you have with the procurement administration during your tenure as the chief of research and development. "A. I had none because there are two parallel administrations at the same level." This General is not in procurement. However, he is being used in such a fashion. He worked parallel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, because we dealt with the procurement, I'd forgotten that the witness said he had no connection with procurement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, you see, unfortunately Ms. Carter is bolder in her assertion than she necessarily should be because that was dealing with a particular period of time, and since we are talking about the general issue of procurement, that is a slightly different issue. But I would like to -- I would like to remind all of us of some words that were spoken but a few days ago on the 15th of July by Mr. Harmon in which he was having some resistance from the Defence with regard to the issue of some documents and we were dealing with procedural matters, and Mr. Harmon took the position that in the fairness to the Prosecution and in order to have a fair trial there are times when the substantive issues that exist override procedural concerns. And I'm only mentioning that because I trust that at least with regard to this team it's a unified team. Whether or not the Prosecution's office chooses to be unified or not really depends, I think, on what the issues are that are presented at the Tribunal. At least with regard to this issue, one would think based upon, as I said before, and I was casting no aspersions whatsoever but rather articulating a well recognised and historically understood legal principle with regard to the duty of the Prosecution that, in terms of the interests of a fair trial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They turned the documents to you pursuant, I'm sure, to Rule 68, that's why you are in possession of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, no. Definitely not Rule 68. They were tendered under Rule 66. If it was tendered under Rule 68, it would be, as I'm sure you can appreciate, in a much different kind of situation. A Rule 68 document by definition is exculpatory. This was not tendered under Rule 68, it was tendered under a different Rule, therefore they obviously found it at some point to be inculpatory. But I am not going to get into, at this moment, the niceties of that particular theme.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The point is that they tendered the documents over to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At least --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: At least they didn't withhold, and I'm not suggesting that they did. Whether or not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are talking about what Mr. Harmon said sometime in July, Mr. Guy-Smith. As we can understand, we are not going to be able to remember that. What was the ruling of the Chamber on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: On that occasion, the Chamber let Mr. Harmon proceed with the introduction of, I believe it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you give us a specific reference of that occasion on the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. It would be pages 12808 et seq., and this was in regard to the interest of General Kovacevic. Mr. Harmon said, "Your Honour --" at line 15 on page 12808: "Your Honour, we did not call General Kovacevic to testify. We did not make the -- we did not introduce these documents obviously until he came. I think the interest of justice is something that we must put above all in terms of the technicalities of whether or not we introduce these or not." Then he went on with the reason why he felt these documents to be relevant. So I mean, one would hope that there would be equal application when dealing with such things as the interest of justice. With regard to the view here, and I'm dealing with this in a slightly different fashion just for the moment, with regard to the view that the Prosecution would take as regards to the interests of justice. If one forwards an argument in which they advocate treatment which they put under the rubric of the interests of justice, then one would assume the self-same party would accept that, especially when dealing with something as we are dealing with here. And once again, I cast no aspersions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you read us the ruling of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, the ruling of the Chamber is: "The Chamber, Moloto dissenting, will grant your application, Mr. Harmon."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, before the Chamber considers, I'd like to point out that the very same language the Defence is relying upon today is the same language that they have sought for the Chamber to reconsider. So it's not as simple as simply reading out a transcript passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The objection is upheld, Judge Picard dissenting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the document that is presently up on the screen, could you tell me, are you familiar with this document? And I don't mean the specific document here, but the type of document that it represents?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm familiar with it because I personally filled out documents with the same contents throughout my military career.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you tell us, if you could, how many of these documents you filled out throughout your military career?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: That pertained mostly to the beginning of my military career when I supervised equipment and warehouses or handed it over to warehouses for the needs of the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe Ms. Carter has something to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to the Defence trying to rehabilitate this document. The witness has been present for the entire legal arguments in relation to the issues with this particular document. To now allow him to answer and be rehabilitated on it would be inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would tend to agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would tend to disagree with the notion of rehabilitation because I'm not seeking to rehabilitate. Based on that particular grounds, since we are dealing with issues of procedure, there is an anticipation here and that anticipation is that I'm going to seek to tender this document again and ask for reconsideration. That is not my intention. If that was my intention, then perhaps the objection may have some purchase independent of whether it's relevant or not. Since that's not my intention and the document is up on the screen, I'm using it for descriptive purposes and to establish a record with regard to this issue and the manner in which it has been treated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It seems -- [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- we are all at cross purposes. I've been advised that the document [Microphone not activated] 815 was admitted and the objection came when 816 was sought to be introduced and that 815 is 448, is D448. Is that our common recollection of the situation?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I had had -- my attempt was to object prior the ruling taking place, however, I was only heard once the exhibit number had already been given. So my microphone was on, I had intended to object, however, procedurally the number was given prior to my objection being heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I think we better roll back the tape, then, because that's not my memory of what occurred. My memory may be incorrect. I think what she did object to is the document that is presently up on the screen. That's what the fight has been about. She did not object to the document beforehand. Otherwise, we would have had had the same spirited conversation we just had with regard to that document that we've just had with regard to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you saying -- that was my feeling too, that 815 wasn't given a number, but the Registrar says it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I thought we have been fighting about 816 this entire time. I didn't think we were fight being 815. I thought -- I didn't think we were fighting about D448, as I understand it to be. I thought we were fighting about this document here, the one that's up on the screen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that 816?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then, I am sorry then, can I just sort of --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Wait a minute, excuse me, excuse me, excuse me. The document on the screen is 815.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is the document that we've been fighting about. That's true. My apologies. I was a tab off in my book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then if it is -- if a ruling was on that 815, the document -- you can't carry on talking about it again. You can talk about documents of similar nature --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't understand why I can't continue talking about this document independent of the issue of whether or not it's been admitted or not. I know of no rule under the guide-lines or other rule that disallows that. But if that is the Court's -- if that's the Court's ruling with regard to this particular document, then I will abide by the Court's ruling because I have no desire to disrespect the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any response to that, Madam Carter?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I leave it to the Court's discretion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You indicated that during the beginning of your military career you filled out a number -- you indicated at page 43, line 1, that in the beginning of your military career when you supervised equipment in the warehouse or handed it over to warehouses for the needs of services, you worked with this particular document. And I asked you if you could tell us about how many of these documents over that period of time you filled out. That may be a kind of a silly question because I assume that it falls in the neighbourhood of a substantial number of documents, but can you guesstimate for us how many of these you filled out, how familiar you with this form?

utterances.speaker: RADOJICA KADIJEVIC
utterances.text: It was a huge number because while I was on a ship for three years, whatever I requested, be it spare parts, fuel, any other equipment or any surplus that I had to return, was accompanied by this document. So anything I received and anything I gave back was accompanied by this document. There was no other way to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
